name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
answer: An AI enablement audit in healthcare examines whether a clinical or operational setting can safely adopt, run, and oversee artificial intelligence systems. It covers model inventory, intended use, data flows, integration points with electronic health records, and the people and processes around each system. The audit is not a one-time technical check, it is a structured review of readiness across clinical, technical, and administrative layers. It typically distinguishes between models used for diagnosis, triage, documentation, scheduling, and back-office work because each carries different risk.

sections.body: An AI enablement audit in healthcare examines whether a clinical or operational setting can safely adopt, run, and oversee artificial intelligence systems. It covers model inventory, intended use, data flows, integration points with electronic health records, and the people and processes around each system. The audit is not a one-time technical check, it is a structured review of readiness across clinical, technical, and administrative layers. It typically distinguishes between models used for diagnosis, triage, documentation, scheduling, and back-office work because each carries different risk.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit looks at the hardware, software, and network environment where models run, including on-premises servers, cloud services, and edge devices such as ultrasound carts or bedside monitors. It checks whether the infrastructure can support model latency, logging, failover, and access control, and whether patient data stays within approved boundaries. It also reviews interfaces with electronic health records, picture archiving systems, and laboratory information systems, since a model is only as reliable as the data it receives in production.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Auditors typically map each AI system from vendor or development source through deployment, then test it against the organization's stated use case and clinical workflow. They review training data summaries, performance reports, version histories, and change management records, and they run limited validation on local patient data where permitted. The work often follows a checklist that pairs technical checks with interviews of clinical, IT, compliance, and supply chain staff, because failures usually come from handoffs rather than the model itself.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: This section covers rights, risk, and provenance. The audit asks who owns the model, what data it was trained on, what regulatory status it holds, and what liability and indemnity terms exist in vendor contracts. It also checks whether the organization has a clear process for reporting model errors, disabling a model, and notifying patients or regulators when harm occurs. Provenance and contract review are treated as core evidence, not background reading.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The AI enablement audit is moving from a project-based review toward continuous monitoring tied to model registries and incident logs. As more models are embedded in routine care, auditors are being asked to track drift, retraining, and downstream effects on staff workload and patient outcomes. The likely direction is a standing audit function that updates with each model version and each change in clinical workflow, rather than a single pre-deployment gate.
